stories.title: Digging in the Dirt With Harold and His Giant Pumpkins
stories.summary: 13-year-old Harold Harris grew two giant pumpkins from seeds his grandparents gifted him — one weighing 340 pounds and the other estimated over 400. He tracks their growth daily with math and a whole lot of water.
stories.extended_summary: Most kids spend summer break sleeping in. Harold Harris spent his watering a pumpkin patch with up to 100 gallons a day. The 13-year-old from Edgartown, Massachusetts, planted giant pumpkin seeds from his grandparents and ended up with two monsters: one weighing 340 pounds and another estimated at over 400. At peak growth, they packed on 27 pounds a day. Harold tracks every inch with daily measurements and a conversion table he built himself. 'It's usually within five percent accuracy,' he says. It's part science project, part obsession — and proof that big things can come from small beginnings.

stories.title: From the streets to the suites
stories.summary: Chef Pat Gray went from selling plates to barbershops while in culinary school to running Chef Pat's Kitchen and catering for stars like Usher and Lil Wayne. Her journey? 'From the streets to the suites.'
stories.extended_summary: Before she was catering for Usher and Lil Wayne, Patricia Gray was hustling plates to barbershops and beauty salons along Goodfellow Boulevard. She was in culinary school, raising a daughter, and needed income to cover 365 hours of unpaid training. So she started selling small plates with a simple pitch: 'I'm trying to start my own business. If you like it, support me.' They did. Today, Chef Pat runs Chef Pat's Kitchen on the same North St. Louis corridor, plus a catering business that's fed the O'Jays, Chris Brown, and more. Musiq Soulchild calls her 'one of the greatest in the game.'

stories.summary: Jason Winter, already known for making some of America's best pizza, is now selling nearly 900 sourdough bagels every weekend from his Little Ugly's stand in Long Beach. They're fermented for 48 hours and topped with local koji cream cheese.
stories.extended_summary: Jason Winter already had a reputation for making some of the best pizza in America. Now he's added another title: bagel guy. Every weekend, his Little Ugly's stand at 4th and Termino in Long Beach draws crowds for sourdough bagels that are unyeasted, fermented for 48 hours, and topped with koji-inoculated cream cheese and Sun Gold tomatoes. Last weekend alone, he sold nearly 900. 'Tender, tangy, crackly, just chewy enough,' is how L.A. TACO describes them. It's a side hustle that's quickly becoming a main event.

stories.title: Heirloom helps real estate agents and heirs with complexities of inherited properties
stories.summary: Alexa Rosario built Heirloom, a platform that helps families and real estate agents navigate inherited properties with dignity. She's trained over 1,500 agents on how to protect family legacies during probate.
stories.extended_summary: After spending 2.5 years in probate with her own family, Alexa Rosario knew the system was broken. So she built Heirloom, a Davie-based platform that trains real estate agents to handle inherited properties with care — from the language they use to the vendors they bring in for estate cleanups. Over 1,500 agents have gone through her program, learning how to market homes that still hold a family's belongings and memories. 'We train the agents to market the properties differently than you would a traditional real estate transaction,' Rosario says. Her goal: protect family legacies during one of life's hardest transitions.

stories.title: In old NASA data, scientists find a surprising new type of cosmic object
stories.summary: Scientists found a new class of 'hypersoft' X-ray beacons hiding in 18 years of old NASA Chandra data. These luminous objects could be precursors to supernovas or even triple-star systems with black holes.
stories.extended_summary: For nearly two decades, NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory collected data that sat waiting. Now, scientists have found something unexpected in it: a whole new class of 'hypersoft' X-ray beacons in nearby galaxies. 'They are very luminous,' says Mustafa Muhibullah, the University of Alabama grad student who led the research. 'They are numerous in galaxies.' Some could be precursors to exploding stars. Others might be exotic triple-star systems where two stars have collapsed into black holes. The discovery, pulled from data collected between 1999 and 2017, could help solve some of astronomy's biggest mysteries.

stories.title: Meet the Denver chef who opened 3 Michelin star restaurants in 3 years
stories.summary: Chef Johnny Curiel and his wife Kasie sold their house to open their first restaurant. Three years later, they've opened six spots and earned three Michelin stars — including Colorado's only star this year.
stories.extended_summary: Chef Johnny Curiel and his wife Kasie sold their house to open their first restaurant. That gamble paid off: Alma Fonda Fina earned Colorado's only Michelin star the following year. Since then, the couple has opened six restaurants in three years, with three earning Michelin recognition — including their newest spot, Milpero, which got a star after just four months of service. Curiel, who grew up in Guadalajara surrounded by chefs, says there's no formula. Menus change with the seasons, the weather, or a really good crudo he ate in Mexico. His rise from house-selling risk to Michelin mainstay borders on mystical — but it's really just relentless craft.

stories.title: Survivors Build Database Of Accused Protestant Clergy Abusers
stories.summary: Survivors of church abuse launched Protestant Accountability, a database listing over 2,700 accused clergy members across 100+ denominations. The goal: expose hidden abuse and protect those at risk.
stories.extended_summary: A new database called Protestant Accountability is pulling back the curtain on abuse within the Christian church. Launched in August by survivors, it lists over 2,700 accused or convicted individuals across more than 100 denominations — including photos, positions held, and supporting documentation. It also names those who enabled or covered up abuse. The nonprofit's leadership is almost entirely made up of survivors, including president Chellee Taylor, who won a 2022 settlement from the Southern Baptist Convention. 'I don't want to burn it down,' Taylor told Christianity Today. 'I want to make it better.' The database is a tool for transparency, accountability, and protection.

stories.title: UC Merced Team Earns Best Paper Award at SenSys 2026
stories.summary: A UC Merced team won Best Paper at SenSys 2026 for SoilX, a wireless sensing system that measures six soil properties in real time without recalibration. It could help farmers get accurate data faster and cheaper.
stories.extended_summary: Soil sensors have always had a catch: move them to a new field, and you have to send samples to a lab and wait weeks for recalibration. A UC Merced team just solved that. Their system, SoilX, uses a machine-learning technique called Contrastive Cross-Component Learning and a pyramid-shaped antenna array to measure six soil properties — moisture, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, organic carbon, and texture — in real time, in any orientation. Tested across five soil types, it reduced errors by up to 31.5 percent compared to the best existing system. The work won the sole Best Paper Award at SenSys 2026, selected from 505 submissions. For farmers, it means faster, cheaper, more accurate data.

stories.title: ‘No limits’ ministry creates community for adults with disabilities
stories.summary: Benjamin Cantrell, who has cerebral palsy, wondered why young adults with disabilities couldn't have the same fellowship his sister found at church. That question became No Limits, a ministry at Second Baptist in Clinton, Tennessee that grew from 10 members to more than 60 in under a year — and brought 10 new families into the congregation.
stories.extended_summary: Benjamin Cantrell asked a simple question at dinner one night: why couldn't there be a young adult group for people like him? His sister had found community at Second Baptist's Young Adult Ministries. He wanted the same. His dad, Dail, had been trying to build something like it since Benjamin was in high school — a program for teens and adults with intellectual and physical disabilities — but it never got off the ground. This time it did. No Limits launched in August 2024 with 10 members. Today it has more than 60, offering fellowship both inside and outside the church, and 10 families have joined the congregation because of it. For Benjamin, it's not charity. It's the social life he always deserved.
